author: A Robot
objectives: Students will describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including the eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Students will explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Students will contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Students will predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
Students will compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: This module demonstrates the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as observed from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to the apparent motion of Mars from Earth.
clips.narration: From our perspective on Earth, planets like Mars appear to move against the background stars. Normally, they drift eastward.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars begins to slow its eastward motion.
clips.narration: However, due to the relative motion of our orbits, Mars appears to slow down in its eastward path.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars appears to reverse direction, entering retrograde motion.
clips.narration: Soon, Mars appears to stop and reverse its direction, moving westward against the stars. This is apparent retrograde motion.
Mars continues this westward loop for a couple of months before its apparent motion changes again.
Finally, Mars appears to slow its westward path, stop, and resume its original eastward drift against the stars.
